reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A common, benign, usually self-limiting inflammation of the episclera presenting with acute redness and mild discomfort or grittiness rather than severe pain
Redness may be sectoral or diffuse with a bright red appearance, and visual acuity is preserved
The superficial episcleral vessels blanch with topical phenylephrine, unlike the deeper vessels of scleritis
Classified as simple (diffuse) or nodular; in nodular disease a mobile, tender nodule is seen over the sclera
Most cases are idiopathic, though a minority are linked to systemic inflammatory conditions such as gout, rosacea, or connective-tissue disease
It is distinguished from scleritis by the absence of deep boring pain, vessel blanching with phenylephrine, and a benign course
Management is largely reassurance with lubricants; topical or short courses of oral NSAIDs and, occasionally, mild topical steroids help troublesome or nodular cases
reference.pathophysiology: Episcleritis is inflammation confined to the episclera, the thin vascular layer of connective tissue between the conjunctiva and the sclera. The process is typically a localised, non-granulomatous inflammatory response affecting the superficial episcleral vascular plexus, producing vasodilatation and mild oedema without the deep scleral destruction of true scleritis. It is usually idiopathic and self-limiting, though recurrent or nodular episodes can occasionally be associated with systemic inflammatory disease.
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination and topical phenylephrine test to confirm superficial vessel involvement
Assessment of visual acuity to confirm it is preserved
Limited systemic workup only in recurrent, nodular, or atypical cases (e.g. inflammatory markers, autoimmune screen, urate)
redFlags: Severe boring pain, deep violaceous vessels, or failure to blanch with phenylephrine suggesting scleritis instead
Reduced visual acuity, which should not occur in simple episcleritis
Frequently recurrent disease suggesting an underlying systemic inflammatory condition
reference.prognosis: Episcleritis is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving within one to two weeks without lasting visual consequences, although recurrences are common.
pitfalls: Confusing episcleritis with scleritis and over-investigating or over-treating a benign condition
Conversely, dismissing genuine scleritis as episcleritis and missing sight-threatening disease
Prolonged unnecessary topical steroid use with its attendant risks of raised intraocular pressure
Overlooking an associated systemic disease in recurrent cases
management: Reassure the patient, as episcleritis is benign and usually self-limiting, often needing no active treatment
Relieve symptoms with ocular lubricants, artificial tears and cold compresses
Use topical or oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for troublesome discomfort, and a short course of topical corticosteroid for persistent or nodular disease
Investigate and treat an underlying systemic association in recurrent, nodular or atypical cases, such as gout, rosacea or connective-tissue disease
Distinguish from scleritis using the topical phenylephrine blanching test, and escalate to ophthalmology if there is deep boring pain or reduced vision suggesting scleritis
